extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate practitioners, IP counsel, law clerks
extracted.subtask_description: A compilation of Federal Circuit standards and legal criteria for evaluating jurisdiction, venue, standing, procedural preservation, jury instructions, and related patent-litigation issues. Intended to guide practitioners on when appeals lie, how to preserve issues, what constitutes standing/personal jurisdiction, and commodity-specific requirements (e.g., ITC domestic-industry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral Order Doctrine conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a district court order to come within the collateral order exception, it must at a minimum satisfy three conditions: [1] 'conclusively determine the disputed question,' [2] 'resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits of the action,' and [3] 'be effectively unreviewable on appeal from a final judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The collateral order doctrine is a limited exception to the general requirement that appellate jurisdiction arises only after a final order. A preliminary or non-conclusive ruling (e.g., court holding record inadequate to decide immunity) does not meet the 'conclusive determination' requirement and thus is not immediately appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific personal jurisdiction — purposeful direction and relatedness
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant must have sufficient contacts with the forum such that it purposefully directed activities at the forum and the action arises out of or relates to those forum-directed activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted enforcement activities (e.g., submitting an APEX report to Amazon with an intended effect on a Utah seller) can constitute purposeful direction when the filing's intended effect would necessarily affect marketing and sales in the forum. Sending communications from another state (e.g., to Amazon in Washington) does not defeat a finding of direction if the action was aimed at a forum resident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III standing (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff must show (1) an injury in fact, (2) fairly traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic case-or-controversy test for federal-court jurisdiction. Failure to establish any of the three elements (e.g., no injury, speculative future harms) deprives the court of jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee/exclusionary-rights inquiry for standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a party has Article III standing turns on whether it retains an exclusionary right—i.e., whether infringement would invade the party's legally protected interest—and not on whether the party is a 'patentee' under 35 U.S.C. § 281, which is not a jurisdictional requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry focuses on the actual transfer of rights at the time the complaint was filed. Hypothetical or potential redistributions of rights (e.g., options in a security agreement not exercised) do not, without more, divest the owner of all exclusionary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of security interests/options on exclusionary rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A security interest or the secured party's options upon default (including options to license or enforce) do not automatically divest the debtor/patent owner of exclusionary rights absent evidence that the secured party elected/exercised those rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether, in practice or by actual transfer/election, the secured party has obtained the exclusionary rights. Mere contractual ability or option is insufficient to show lack of standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of employment assignment 'entirely on my own time' exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous contract language (e.g., the phrase 'developed entirely on my own time') does not unambiguously assign inventions; courts must inquire into mutual intent and surrounding facts rather than resolve such ambiguity on summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the phrase's ordinary meaning allows multiple reasonable interpretations (limited to on-the-clock work vs. broader notions of accountability), further factual inquiry is required and summary judgment is inappropriate; factfinding may be necessary to resolve standing/ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to appeal PTAB decisions (Federal Circuit jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: To appeal a PTAB final written decision to the Federal Circuit, the appellant must demonstrate Article III standing (injury in fact, traceability, redressability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB appearances do not by themselves satisfy Article III; an appellant relying on potential future infringement must show concrete plans creating a substantial likelihood of future infringement or suit. Vague/conclusory declarations and speculative possibilities (including letters predating district-court dismissals with prejudice) are insufficient to establish standing to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayh–Dole 'subject invention' and 'funding agreement' criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Bayh–Dole, a 'contractor' is a party to a 'funding agreement' (contract, grant, or cooperative agreement with a Federal agency for R&D), and an 'invention' is any invention conceived or first actually reduced to practice in performance of work under a funding agreement; subject inventions give the government certain license rights under 35 U.S.C. § 201 and § 202(c)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work performed under subcontracts may be 'in the performance of work under a funding agreement' even if subcontract paperwork is executed after the work began; courts recognize backward-reaching payment practices and will analyze whether the work was covered by the funding agreement in substance, not merely by execution dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation-by-reference in appellate briefs limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may not incorporate by reference arguments into one brief from another unless in compliance with Fed. R. App. P. 28, and in no event is such incorporation permitted if it would result in exceeding the applicable word count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-referencing multiple briefs to 'enhance efficiency' or 'stream-line briefing' is improper if it violates precedent (e.g., Microsoft) or procedural rules. Counsel should withdraw improper incorporations once aware; failing to do so may result in admonishment or sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum-selection clause scope and IPR filings
rubrics_metrics.description: A forum-selection clause in a settlement/license agreement can apply to the entire term of the agreement; however, if the agreement expressly allows filing of IPRs during a covenant period under certain circumstances, the clause cannot be read to categorically prohibit IPR filings after the covenant period merely because it restricted suits during the covenant period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine the agreement's language as a whole. Preliminary-injunction requests based on forum-selection clauses must still satisfy the usual injunction factors (likelihood of success, irreparable harm, balance of hardships, public interest). Active participation in IPRs before seeking an injunction can negate a finding of irreparable harm; inconsistent positions about licensing may affect the balance of hardships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving evidentiary issues for appeal (motion in limine vs. trial objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a motion in limine does not preserve an evidentiary issue for appeal when the party fails to object to the evidence at trial; a contemporaneous trial objection is generally required to preserve the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow circuit-specific preservation rules (e.g., Fifth Circuit authority cited): make contemporaneous objections at trial even if a motion in limine has been filed, or risk waiver of the issue on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury instructions on objective indicia of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury instructions addressing objective indicia (secondary considerations) must encompass all indicia for which there is evidence (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need, industry praise, copying, licensing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting evidence-supported indicia can render instructions erroneous and prejudicial, warranting remand. Parties should request tailored instructions that reference the specific indicia in the record, and courts must ensure instructions read to the jury include those indicia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony and disclosure limits on objective indicia
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert may be limited to testifying on topics disclosed in his/her expert report; testimony on objective indicia not disclosed in the report may be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should assess whether expert reports adequately disclose opinions on specific indicia; allowing an expert to testify on ultimate issues without proper disclosure for components of objective indicia can be error. Parties must ensure expert reports cover all topics they intend the expert to address at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of a party's patent as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of a party's own patent may be admissible for limited purposes such as willfulness and damages; it is not per se inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court can permit such evidence while providing limiting instructions to the jury on the purpose for which the evidence may be considered (e.g., only for willfulness/damages and not for infringement).

rubrics_metrics.name: ITC Section 337 'domestic industry' economic prong
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain relief under Section 337, a complainant must show that 'an industry in the United States, relating to the articles protected by the patent, ... exists or is in the process of being established.' Expenditures must be 'sufficiently substantial investment in the exploitation of the intellectual property.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission evaluates whether investments are attributable to the functionality necessary to practice the patent. Aggregating investments across multiple products that practice different patents without allocating investments to each asserted patent/product group undermines the evidentiary basis for the economic prong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-by-patent allocation for aggregated investments
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complainant's domestic products practice different patents or combinations of patents, the complainant may need to establish separate domestic industries (and allocate investments) for each relevant patent or patent group rather than aggregate investments across unrelated products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregation is permissible only where the products relate to the same patent(s). If a complainant aggregates investments across products that practice multiple different patents, the Commission may require breakdowns to evaluate the significance of investments with respect to each asserted patent.
